From left: HKMA's chief executive Eddie Yue, Denis Beau, Tommaso Mancini-Griffoli, and Georges Elhedery at the Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK 2026 on Monday. HSBC chief executive Georges Elhedery said the bank will sign a partnership agreement tomorrow to establish an AI & Emerging Technology Institute in Hong Kong, with Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) as its first anchor academic partner. Speaking at the Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK 2026, Elhedery said the bank realized early on that artificial intelligence would bring disruptive impact, transforming and eliminating various roles while creating entirely new ones. The bank's first priority is to bring all 200,000 colleagues on the journey with them, rather than creating an environment full of uncertainty, he added. Elhedery said the AI vision set out earlier comprises three major goals – empowering all colleagues through AI training and AI tools, redesigning operational processes and procedures in rethinking how to conduct KYC and customer due diligence, reshaping fraud detection, anti-financial crime detection, and credit approval, and providing personalized services to clients, with the bank now testing conversations between clients' AI agents and the bank's agents. Tokenized Gold and Stablecoin Scale Up. On tokenization, Elhedery said the tokenized gold launched earlier has become one of the top three tokenized gold instruments globally, and noted that the bank's Hong Kong dollar-denominated stablecoin RedCoin was officially launched last week and already has 50,000 users, with a target of millions. The current growth trend is positive, he noted, clearly demonstrating that as long as the technology is sound and secure, with a well-developed regulatory environment, emerging technologies can absolutely achieve scale. Quantum Transition to Take Three to Five Years. As for quantum computing, Elhedery said the vast majority of current cryptographic methods are vulnerable to being cracked by quantum computing. He estimated a transition period of three to five years to move existing encryption systems to methods more resistant to quantum attacks, while also needing the agility to switch between different encryption methods to continuously maintain quantum resilience. BIS Innovation Hub Studies Tokenization Benefits. Meanwhile, Tommaso Mancini-Griffoli, head of the BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH), the unit under the Bank for International Settlements, said BISIH is studying how tokenization can help central banks optimize monetary policy operations. Through tokenization, new liquidity channels can be structured in much shorter time periods, which is particularly important during times of market volatility, he said. The hub is also studying how to reduce compliance costs by automating compliance through tokenization. Mancini-Griffoli said challenges such as governance and risk management take time to resolve. He cited "Nexus," a cross-border payment project BIS is running with multiple Asian countries that aims to link fast payment systems, noting that it spent about a year testing technological solutions and another year devising governance arrangements and other related matters. Supervisory Focus Turns to Control, Trust and AI Oversight. Banque de France's first deputy governor Denis Beau said the key question today is no longer whether financial institutions should use AI, but whether they reflect on control and trust so that this profile is not hard to manage. title: Why Morgan Stanley is turning advisors loose to build their own AI agents
excerpt: Wealth management. Why Morgan Stanley is turning advisors loose to build their own AI agents. By Dan Shaw. About Dan. twitter. FinancialDan2. mailto. dan. shaw@arizent. com. linkedin. dan-shaw-97105844/. Published November 02, 2026, 2:23 p. m. EST. 8 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: Unlike many firms that simply provide AI agents for wealth management, Morgan Stanley lets advisors try building their own. The 50,000 attempts made so far have yielded mixed results. Expert quote: "If you want to build your own agent, and if you have a level of knowledge and complexity, the world is your oyster. " — Koren Maranca, AI head for Morgan Stanley's wealth management division. At Morgan Stanley, advisors aren't restricted to using just AI agents and other systems devised for them by the firm. They can also go out and make their own. So far, Morgan Stanley advisors have made nearly 50,000 attempts using natural-language prompts to produce AI agents designed in large part to give them more time with clients by automating routine tasks. "If you want to build your own agent, and if you have a level of knowledge and complexity, the world is your oyster," said Koren Maranca, head of artificial intelligence for Morgan Stanley's wealth management division. "And you can curate any agent that's going to be impactful to you and your team. ". Maranca said advisors have built agents specifically to track portfolio holdings that are of particular interest to their clients. "Or it could be something more complex of looking across their book and pulling in all of the outgoing flows over a certain amount every day and delivering that information to them at a certain period of time on a daily basis," she said. READ MORE: AI could take advisors back 3 decades. That's a good thing. Why most of the new AI agents don't pass the test. Of course, that's not to say anywhere near the majority of those 50,000 agents are in day-to-day use. As is the case with most technological experiments, most don't make it past early testing. Maranca said agents that prove useful enough to be embraced by many people on an advisor's team are subjected to careful reviews to make sure the answers they provide are both accurate and complete. Agents that seem promising enough for possible adoption throughout the firm are put through even more extensive testing. But doing all that for 50,000 agents, most of which never going anywhere, would be impossible. "Sometimes people build an agent, they use it twice, and then they never touch it again," Maranca said. "So we're not going through comprehensive reviews for an orphaned agent. But those agents that we see are actually being incorporated into an advisor's practice, those go through a review and approval post-use. ". Morgan Stanley was one of the earliest large wealth managers to enter into a contract with one of the big AI companies. Within months of OpenAI's release of its ChatGPT large language model in 2022, Morgan Stanley had brokered an agreement bringing the burgeoning technology to its advisors. READ MORE: 4 ways to tell if your AI research tool is fudging the numbers. How Morgan Stanley uses AI to cut down on call center queries. Beyond giving advisors leeway to tinker with AI independently, the firm has devised its AI @ Morgan Stanley, or AI@MS, to develop a set of agents designed to help in various common financial-planning situations. Some of the most popular agents available to all advisors at Morgan Stanley offer assistance in everything from providing answers to financial-planning questions that previously would have gone to an internal call center to organizing an advisor's day to projecting income from a high-yielding savings account. Maranca said many of the uses Morgan Stanley initially found for AI@MS four years ago "are now commonplace" among wealth management firms. title: HKMA launches Project SAGE on agentic finance, names expert group
excerpt: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has launched Project SAGE to support the responsible development and adoption of agentic finance in Hong Kong, as the regulator moves to formalise governance around AI systems that can act on users' behalf in financial services. Evidence and context. In a press release dated 2 November 2026, the HKMA said Project SAGE stands for “Securing Agentic Finance with Governance and Enablement. ” The authority said the initiative is intended to enable practical applications of agentic finance while ensuring that a governance framework is in place. It added that, as agentic AI technologies mature, the financial industry is moving beyond internal adoption to explore how AI agents may make financial services more efficient and secure. The HKMA said Project SAGE will focus on four areas: market development and use-case exploration; agent identity; interoperability standards; and legal and regulatory frameworks. Under market development, the authority said potential applications include business-to-consumer uses such as agentic commerce and everyday payments, business-to-business use cases such as procurement and treasury management, and machine-to-machine payments for digital services. On identity, the HKMA said it will explore approaches to verifying AI agents' identities and delegated authority, including Know Your Agent practices and authentication mechanisms. On standards, it will facilitate discussion of interoperability-related protocols to support secure and seamless interactions across the ecosystem. On regulation, it said it will exchange views on governance arrangements, liability and consumer protection. To support the work, the HKMA has established the Agentic Finance Expert Group. The authority said the group includes stakeholders from financial institutions, technology service providers, professional service firms and academia. HKMA Chief Executive Eddie Yue said agentic finance “has the potential to transform how financial services are delivered and utilised,” adding that the initiatives aim to foster innovation while reinforcing Hong Kong's role in next-generation financial technology and safeguarding the stability of the financial system. The announcement did not disclose a timetable for implementation or identify any specific pilot outcomes from Project SAGE. It also said the effort is designed to help the HKMA and industry navigate both the opportunities and the risks associated with agentic finance. hkma. hong kong. artificial intelligence. fintech. title: HSBC expands artificial intelligence footprint across Asia with new Hong Kong institute
excerpt: Next-Gen Technologies. 4 min Read. HSBC expands artificial intelligence footprint across Asia with new Hong Kong institute. HSBC will launch an artificial intelligence and emerging technology institute in Hong Kong by the first quarter of 2027, following a similar venture in Singapore. The expansion reflects banking sector-wide acceleration in AI adoption, which is prompting job cuts at rivals like Citi and Barclays while creating specialist roles. Hong Kong's regulator has announced Project SAGE to establish safeguards for AI agent deployment in finance. ETCIOSEA. Published On Nov 02, 2026 at 08:14 PM IST. Select ETCIOSEA as Preferred Choice on Google. HSBC is making a substantial bet on artificial intelligence by establishing a dedicated institute in Hong Kong , signalling the bank’s intention to position itself at the forefront of emerging technology adoption across Asia. The bank announced during Hong Kong’s FinTech Week that it plans to open the facility in the first quarter of 2027, with ambitious long-term plans to relocate the centre to Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis once infrastructure becomes available. Georges Elhedery, HSBC’s Group Chief Executive, made the announcement on Monday, emphasising the strategic importance of the move. The institute will serve as a hub for AI research and development, building on earlier momentum the bank established in Singapore, where it began recruiting artificial intelligence specialists in mid-2026. Scaling investment to match competitive landscape. The Hong Kong institute represents part of HSBC’s broader strategy to embed artificial intelligence across its global operations. Elhedery disclosed that the bank is rolling out AI training across its worldwide workforce of approximately 200,000 people, with a particular emphasis on preparing staff for roles that will be reshaped by automation and algorithmic decision-making. Hong Kong University of Science and Technology will serve as the anchor academic partner for the institute, though HSBC did not reveal staffing numbers or initial budget allocations for the venture. The collaboration signals a commitment to research-led innovation rather than purely commercial development, placing the bank among global financial institutions investing in university partnerships to develop next-generation AI capabilities. The Singapore launch earlier in 2026 already positioned HSBC to hire more than 100 AI specialists. The Hong Kong institute will complement this effort and allow the bank to tap into the city’s deep reservoir of engineering talent and academic expertise. Broader industry shift toward automation and workforce restructuring. HSBC’s move reflects a wider pattern of technological disruption sweeping through global banking. Institutions including Citi, Standard Chartered, and Barclays announced significant job reduction programmes during 2026, attributing the cuts to AI-driven operational efficiencies and structural changes in how financial services are delivered. The contrast between these reductions and HSBC’s expansion in AI hiring shows that while some roles disappear, new specialist positions emerge, though typically requiring different skill sets than traditional banking roles. Elhedery acknowledged this reality candidly during the conference. “AI is going to be disruptive. It’s going to transform jobs,” he stated, recognising that the technology will alter the nature of work across the financial sector. His comments underscore management’s awareness that artificial intelligence will necessitate workforce adaptation and retraining at scale. HSBC operates with approximately 28,000 staff members in Hong Kong alone and maintains one of the largest private-sector workforces in the city. Regulators move to establish guardrails for AI adoption. As banks accelerate AI deployment, Hong Kong’s regulatory authorities are establishing frameworks to manage associated risks. title: HSBC Hong Kong AI Hub: 4 Key Areas Set for Research
excerpt: HSBC Hong Kong AI Hub: 4 Key Areas Set for Research. HSBC will open an AI institute in Hong Kong in Q1 2027 with HKUST. The hub will focus on AI safety, fraud detection, post-quantum cryptography and blockchain, strengthening the bank's technology push across Asia. Written By:. Simran Mishra. Reviewed By:. Manisha Sharma. Published on : 02 Nov 2026, 11:16 am. Updated on : 02 Nov 2026, 11:16 am. Copied. HSBC plans to open a new AI institute in Hong Kong during the first quarter of 2027. CEO Georges Elhedery announced the expansion at Hong Kong Fintech Week, highlighting the bank's growing investment in artificial intelligence. The institute will work with the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) to develop emerging technologies for banking. The Hong Kong AI hub will expand HSBC's regional technology network following its Singapore center launch earlier this year. The bank aims to connect academic research with practical banking applications through the new institute. It will initially operate in Hong Kong before moving to the Northern Metropolis development zone. The institute will focus on artificial intelligence, emerging technologies and workforce development. Its research priorities include AI safety, fraud detection, post-quantum cryptography and blockchain applications. HSBC also plans to strengthen its ability to introduce advanced technologies across financial services. The expansion follows HSBC's July announcement about its Singapore AI hub. The bank planned to recruit more than 100 AI specialists for that center. Together, both locations could strengthen HSBC's technology capabilities across two major Asian financial markets. Elhedery acknowledged the technology's impact on employment during his conference remarks. "AI is going to be disruptive. It's going to transform jobs," he said. His comments reflect growing changes across banking as financial institutions increase automation and rethink workforce requirements. Meanwhile, Hong Kong regulators are preparing safeguards for wider AI adoption across financial services. Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Eddie Yue announced Project SAGE to support responsible AI agent development. The initiative will examine governance, accountability and standards for trusted AI agents. Around 80% of Hong Kong banks have already adopted AI or generative AI, according to Yue. The regulator also plans expert consultations and testing to assess how AI agents operate across financial institutions. Bank of America is warning customers that they could be on the hook for what happens if they hand their banking logins to an AI agent. In an email to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the AI World,” the bank urges people to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, reports TechCrunch. The warning specifically covers “an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf. ”. A Bank of America spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the email, which was first posted on social media, is real. The bank also tells customers that the risk falls on them if they share their logins anyway. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access. ”. Handing a banking password to an AI assistant could let it do things with the customer’s money without them knowing, or lead the bank to lock the account if it thinks someone is breaking in. A security flaw in the AI tool could also leak the login to hackers. Bank of America’s guidance on outside apps says customers should instead use its consent-based option, where they log in directly with the bank and can cut off an app’s access at any time. The bank says the safest way to stop an app that already has a customer’s login is to change the password. The Daily Hodl reported earlier this month that JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley are moving to block or restrict AI agents after finding unauthorized bots inside customer accounts. title: Aion Launches AI Agent for Business Finance, Banking, Payments, Cards & Credit
excerpt: Home > Artificial Intelligence. Artificial Intelligence | November 2, 2026. Aion Launches AI Agent for Business Finance, Banking, Payments, Cards & Credit. The agent takes on the routine work of business finance, from paying bills and following up on invoices to preparing reports for the close. Aion , the finance platform for growing businesses, today launched Aion Agent , an AI agent that takes on the routine work of business finance, from paying bills and following up on invoices to preparing reports for the close. Aion Agent works across Aion’s banking, payments, cards, and credit products, and every payment, submission, and signature it prepares waits for a person on the client’s team to approve it. At growing companies, much of the finance team’s week goes to work that doesn’t call for judgment: sorting bills, chasing invoices, logging in to customer and vendor portals, and keeping the accounting system current. Aion Agent handles that work and brings the team the decisions. Most finance AI tools sit on top of companies’ systems and see only one part of the business. Typically, bill pay tools, receivables software, and accounting add-ons each see one slice of the business, and the work inside customer and vendor portals still falls to a person. Aion Agent is built into the platform where a company’s money already moves, across banking, payments, receivables, and credit. It also has its own browser, so it can handle portal work that other software often can’t reach. For growing companies with lean finance teams, that means less time on routine work and more time for the decisions that grow the business. “Finance teams told us they want the routine work off their desks and the final say left with them,” said Satish Palvai, founder and CEO of Aion. “So, we built Aion Agent to do the work and let the team approve it. Because it runs on the same platform as a client’s banking, payments, and credit, it sees and can act on the full picture, like a finance teammate would. ”. Aion Agent enables teams to grow. Collects what’s owed. Handles billing and collections and submits invoices through Aion or directly in a client’s customer portals. Pays bills and keeps the books current. Lines up bills for approval, pulls invoices and statements from vendor sites, and keeps the accounting system in sync. Handles banking tasks. Prepares transfers and payments across the company’s accounts for the team to approve. Manages cards. Issues cards with the spending limits and restrictions the team set. Works the line of credit. Works with the company’s Aion credit line, with the team approving anything that moves money. Reports on the business. Prepares reports, supports the month-end close, and answers questions about performance, with every figure traced to the transactions behind it. Keeps going in the background. Works toward goals the team sets, learns how each team does things, and notifies approved users when a decision is needed. And since it has its own browser, it works in accounting systems and third-party portals the way a person would—letting the team watch, step in, or hand a task back. Answers questions in Claude, ChatGPT, or Claude in Slack. Once connected, it answers from the client’s Aion accounts and records. A reply in chat never approves anything; money moves only after approval inside Aion. Helps businesses switch. Drafts a payment inventory from a business’s existing statements, and account holders can ask it to email an account verification letter. Always in the finance team’s control. Paying, submitting, signing, and sending all require approval. When the Agent needs to sign in to another system, the client types the credentials into a secure panel in Aion, and the Agent never sees them. title: Happen Bank's Scott Sanborn talks agentic AI and rate risk
excerpt: Happen Bank. Happen Bank's Scott Sanborn talks agentic AI and rate risk. By Melinda Lucy. About Melinda. mailto. melinda. lucy@americanbanker. com. linkedin. melinda-huspen. Published November 02, 2026, 4:01 p. m. EST. 6 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: Happen Bank is currently allowing LLMs to scrape its website content so they will cite the brand to potential customers, but it is also blocking AI agents from accessing bank accounts until regulatory concerns are resolved, according to CEO Scott Sanborn. Supporting data: Sanborn said that Happen Bank's loan delinquencies have been 40% lower than FICO's competitive set for around six years. Despite grappling with rising interest rates and swallowing the costs of a full rebrand, Happen Bank reported that it broke multiple performance records in the third quarter and raised its full-year guidance. Processing Content. "In the quarter, financials as a whole were under a lot of pressure in the public market," Happen Bank CEO Scott Sanborn told American Banker. "There was an expectation that rising rates would really impact our ability to deliver and stay on track with our earnings. You can see with the results that we actually beat expectations and raised the earnings guide. ". American Banker spoke with Sanborn after Happen Bank reported its first full quarter under its new name to discuss the bank's home loan strategy, its approach to AI agents, the current rate environment and the positive provision adjustments Happen has made throughout the year. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. You mentioned in the earnings call that the bank is preparing for external AI agents. Some banks, as we recently reported , are already starting to actively block them. What is Happen Bank's current stance?. When I say we're preparing for them, what I mean by that is that, step one, we're making sure we're visible to those agents and that the content we produce is made available to them. For people searching, which is already an activity happening today, they can find us. Step two is, once they find us, can they act upon us? Right now, that answer is no – similar to what you've heard from other banks, to the extent possible, and without geeking out on it. There are agents that you can quite easily recognize, but if you put OpenClaw on a Mac Mini it looks just like you. That would be hard for anybody to really know. There are some techniques, but it's not foolproof. Where possible, we are blocking today until things like identity, authority, permission and liability are worked out. If somebody gets a loan and then says, "Oh, I didn't mean to get the loan, that agent did it for me," who's at fault here? Does the agent actually have permission to withdraw funds on your behalf? There's a lot of questions that have to be worked out. When I say "getting prepared," we are building the internal infrastructure – let's call it the rails and the harness, if you will, for an agent to be able to ride with the controls built into it. We're doing that for our own internal agent that we're developing and will make available to customers, but we're going to build it in such a way that this could theoretically be repurposed for external agents when the time is right. It's our view that money in motion and people in motion will be very good for our business. We're trying to make it as easy as possible to give them financial rewards for taking action. title: Goldman Sachs Bars Bankers From Employing Some AI Tools
excerpt: Goldman Sachs Bars Bankers From Using Claude Code and GitHub. By PYMNTS | November 2, 2026. |. Goldman Sachs has reportedly instituted a crackdown on artificial intelligence (AI) usage by its bankers. As Bloomberg News reported Monday (Nov. 2), Goldman had for months allowed bankers to use tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub on the job. Now, those tools will be limited to Goldman’s engineers only, according to internal guidance published last month and seen by Bloomberg. A source familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that the ban has frustrated some Goldman traders, who had used AI for things like monitoring client trading flows or creating written and graphic materials. As recently as July, Goldman Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti had touted the “vibe coding” by non-technical employees at Goldman, the report added. Those workers had developed solutions with AI tools and passed on their creations to one of the firm’s 12,000 engineers to enhance, he said in an interview. “We make certain AI tools available to our people to determine the best use cases across different parts of the firm,” Nick Carcaterra , a Goldman spokesperson, told Bloomberg. “After a period of experimentation where we assess a variety of factors including productivity and risk management, we put them in the hands of those who are best suited to leverage them for the long term. ”. The report notes that this is happening at a moment when banks are spending millions on artificial intelligence tools while also trying to determine how to deal with rising concerns related to cost, productivity and cybersecurity risk. JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of “ rogue agents ” and said during a third-quarter earnings call last month that outside AI agents would not be permitted inside the bank. Bank of America followed a day later with a condition instead of a ban. As covered here in October, the bank is placing limits on agents’ access to consumer deposits while it develops protocols that decide which party is liable for a payment an AI authorizes. “By Friday, Citigroup had drawn the same line ,” that report said. “The bank does not let third-party agents log into accounts or transact. ”. In other artificial intelligence news, recent PYMNTS Intelligence research shows that 60% of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) using AI said the technology lets them produce more without taking on new employees. “The findings suggested that AI’s most consequential labor market impact may not be the employees that companies eliminate, but the positions they no longer need to create,” PYMNTS wrote last week. “As automation makes routine work cheaper, the same forces reducing demand for labor may be creating a new market for human judgment and accountability, something harder to automate. ”. title: Wells Fargo wants customers to prove they've revoked AI agents
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. Wells Fargo wants customers to prove they've revoked AI agents. By Penny Crosman. About Penny. twitter. pennycrosman. mailto. penny. crosman@arizent. com. linkedin. pennycrosman. Published November 02, 2026, 12:10 p. m. EST. |. Updated November 02, 2026, 5:00 p. m. EST. 3 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: Wells Fargo appears to be the first bank to start requiring customers to prove they've turned off their AI agents' access to their bank accounts, or else be liable for any rogue AI agent activity. Expert quote: "What if I do everything Wells Fargo says to do, and I've got a pile of evidence that I told that agent to stop doing that thing, yet the agent went rogue because maybe there was an ambiguous direction to it or it just went bad, there's still that question — what happens then?"—Elaine Duffus, senior specialized consultant at Wolters Kluwer. Big banks including JPMorganChase and Wells Fargo have been changing their terms of conditions for online and digital banking users to make it clear that customers are liable for any actions taken by AI agents they've authorized — even when those agents go rogue and do something they were not prompted or authorized to do. Processing Content. Wells Fargo is taking this concept a step farther. An updated version of its online access agreement that takes effect Nov. 24 states, "You are responsible for properly and timely revoking any authorization provided to an AI Agent and taking any necessary further action to cease the AI Agent's activities. You must retain evidence of such revocation and must provide such evidence to us, at our request. Until you notify us of such revocation pursuant to Section 17(d), you remain responsible for all the AI Agent's activities, to the extent permitted by law or regulation. ". In other words, even if a customer tells an AI agent to stop accessing their bank account, they're still on the hook unless they produce evidence that they revoked authorization. In response to several questions about the new policy, including what counts as evidence of revocation, a Wells Fargo spokesman said, "Customers may choose to authorize or revoke an AI agent outside of Wells Fargo. The updated agreement asks customers to keep a record of when an AI agent's authority was revoked, because Wells Fargo may not otherwise have visibility into when that occurred. ". This raises questions of whether it's reasonable to expect consumers to capture such evidence and what banks would accept as evidence. "It's fair for Wells Fargo to want a record of when an agent was cut off, since the bank can't see it," said Douglas Borthwick, a former Morgan Stanley and Standard Chartered executive who hosts the Old Men, New Money podcast. "It isn't realistic to expect customers to produce one. Telling a chatbot to stop leaves nothing in the customer's hands that anyone else can check. ". A screenshot of the chat in which the customer revoked access "shows you asked. It doesn't show the agent stopped, and screenshots are easy to fake. " Borthwick is the founder of a startup, The Insumer Model, that provides wallet authentication for developers and AI agents. Even if a customer revokes her AI agent's access to her bank account and can prove she did so, the consumer may not be covered if the agent goes off script. "What if I do everything Wells Fargo says to do, and I've got a pile of evidence that I told that agent to stop doing that thing, yet the agent went rogue because maybe there was an ambiguous direction to it or it just went bad, there's still that question — what happens then?" Elaine Duffus, senior specialized consultant at Wolters Kluwer, told American Banker. "Who's at fault then? Is it me? Is it the bank? Is it the AI provider? How far do we go down the chain to figure out maybe it was that company's fault or that person's fault that this thing had a mind of its own and went and did something that it wasn't supposed to do. The World Bank Group has identified investments in agricultural surveys and data collection as a critical foundation for artificial intelligence-driven farming in Nigeria and nine other African countries, saying the data could help farmers predict crop yields, detect pests and manage production risks. The global financial institution said integrating agricultural survey data with satellite imagery, weather information, soil maps and other digital resources could transform agricultural decision-making, improve productivity and provide farmers with more targeted advisory services. According to a report on agricultural statistics and artificial intelligence readiness, recent surveys conducted in 10 African countries, including Nigeria, have generated valuable information that could support the development of digital agricultural systems and locally relevant AI applications. The countries covered by the surveys are Burkina Faso, Liberia, Malawi, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Tanzania and Uganda. The surveys were conducted with support from World Bank-financed statistical operations and the 50×2030 Initiative, generating data on farms, crops, agricultural production, livestock, farming practices and the socioeconomic conditions of farming households. The World Bank explained that although the investments were initially designed to strengthen agricultural statistics and support evidence-based policymaking, they could now serve a broader purpose by providing the ground-level information required to develop artificial intelligence applications for agriculture. It noted that satellite imagery, weather systems and soil maps could reveal important information about environmental and agricultural conditions but were not sufficient on their own to establish what was happening on individual farms. According to the report, agricultural surveys provide critical details about crops cultivated, land sizes, inputs used, harvests, production losses and farmers’ access to irrigation, extension services, finance and markets. It said combining such information with other digital data sources could help train and validate AI models for estimating crop yields, identifying production challenges and assessing agricultural risks. The institution cited research involving smallholder maize farms in Uganda, which demonstrated that combining satellite imagery with household survey data produced more accurate crop-yield estimates than relying on satellite imagery alone. The report further explained that integrating agricultural survey observations with rainfall patterns, temperature records, soil maps, market information and administrative records could support the development of systems capable of identifying crops, forecasting harvests, detecting drought stress and directing agricultural extension services to farmers who need them. However, the World Bank cautioned that collecting agricultural data alone would not automatically make Nigeria and other African countries ready to adopt artificial intelligence in farming. It identified reliable digital infrastructure, standardised and interoperable data systems, secure access to information, appropriate governance frameworks and skilled personnel as essential requirements for translating agricultural data into practical AI applications. The report said the World Bank Group’s AI readiness framework was built around four critical requirements: connectivity, computing capacity, context and competency. It explained that while agricultural surveys could provide the local information needed to develop relevant AI systems, countries must also strengthen their digital infrastructure, invest in technical expertise and establish safeguards for responsible deployment of the technology. Three and a half years ago, Bryan Cassidy, an executive vice president at Torrington Savings Bank, opposed introducing artificial intelligence into the bank’s operations. The technology was too new, he believed, for the bank to embrace. Today, Cassidy is helping lead the $1 billion-asset bank’s growing adoption of AI. Employees are using the technology to research policies, summarize information, draft communications and perform other tasks that once required considerably more time. “The biggest piece of it is really we want our employees to work more efficiently,” Cassidy said. “It’s a productivity tool is how we look at it. ” Cassidy’s change of heart reflects a broader shift among Connecticut banks, which are increasingly adopting AI to improve productivity, reduce costs and better serve customers. As adoption grows, however, Connecticut regulators are establishing safeguards intended to protect consumers without discouraging innovation. The state Department of Banking issued draft guidance Sept. 22 calling on banks, credit unions and other regulated financial businesses to adopt formal AI oversight policies, protect sensitive customer information, guard against discriminatory decisions and ensure humans retain control over critical processes. Once finalized, the guidance will establish regulatory expectations, with compliance evaluated during the department’s regular examinations. Connecticut and Michigan are the only two states so far to issue guidance specifically addressing AI use by regulated financial businesses, according to Joseph Chambers, general counsel and chief of staff at the Connecticut Department of Banking. Banking Commissioner Jorge Perez said the guidance will not be a “silver bullet” against risks, but establishing expectations is increasingly important. “This is technology that is changing so fast, and the financial sector is changing so fast,” said Perez, who noted the state’s safeguards will evolve as AI becomes more deeply integrated into financial operations. Consumer advocates and the financial industry itself have also been calling for clearer rules on AI use, Perez said. The work required to meet those expectations will vary. title: iCOMPASS unveils KY-AI platform for Hong Kong bank governance
excerpt: iCOMPASS unveils KY-AI platform for Hong Kong bank governance. November 02, 2026 | 15:38. -->. Tweet. Technology vendor iCOMPASS introduced its KY-AI platform at Hong Kong FinTech Week, helping commercial banks meet HKMA ART Framework guidelines for artificial intelligence risk management. HONG KONG SAR – Media OutReach Newswire – 2 November 2026 – iCOMPASS, the developer of ULTRA™, an AI-powered Compliance Operating System, today introduced KY-AI™ (Know Your Artificial Intelligence) to the Hong Kong market at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026. The announcement follows the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) introduction of its ART Framework on 15 October, sharpening attention on how banks establish accountability, operational resilience and trust as artificial intelligence becomes more autonomous. Financial institutions are moving beyond AI experiments towards tools that analyse sensitive data, recommend decisions and increasingly act across connected systems. Yet a basic governance question remains: can an institution identify where AI is operating, what it is permitted to do, who is accountable and whether its behaviour remains acceptable over time? KY-AI™ turns these questions into a continuous, evidence-based governance process. Built around its Know–Approve–Test–Watch lifecycle, the solution enables financial institutions to identify and understand the AI systems they use, including third-party tools, assess their risks and potential impact, establish clear ownership and accountability, and ensure appropriate approvals and ongoing monitoring are in place. As AI systems evolve, KY-AI™ enables institutions to track material changes, detect emerging risks and intervene when necessary. This transforms AI oversight from a one-time assessment into a continuous, evidence-based governance process that strengthens accountability and builds lasting trust in AI outcomes. "The question is no longer simply whether a financial institution uses AI, but whether management truly understands what each AI system does, the risks involved, who is accountable and when intervention is needed," said Raymond Moh, CEO of iCOMPASS. "With KY-AI™, we are applying the same discipline of knowing your customer to knowing your artificial intelligence. By making AI oversight an ongoing, documented process rather than a one-off exercise, we help financial institutions build greater confidence and trust in how AI is used and the outcomes it delivers. " The introduction builds on iCOMPASS' 6-in-1 ULTRA KYC™ solution, which brings onboarding & identity verification, screening, customer due diligence, risk assessment, ongoing monitoring and change management into a connected, evidence-linked AML/KYC workflow. Having focused on making customer-risk decisions traceable, iCOMPASS is extending the same emphasis on clear ownership, documented decisions and lifecycle monitoring to AI governance. Alongside the KY-AI™ introduction, iCOMPASS is collaborating with Cambridge Advisers Hong Kong under a Memorandum of Understanding to deliver digital compliance training through UltraLearn™. Cambridge Advisers Hong Kong provides regulatory training content while iCOMPASS supplies the learning platform powered by AI, including training records, assessments, reminders and CPT tracking. Courses cover areas including AML, cybersecurity, data protection and professional conduct. iCOMPASS serves more than 100 financial institutions across the region and holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification and a SOC 2 Type II attestation covering all five Trust Services Criteria. title: KB Kookmin Bank to lead $9.45 bil. AI infrastructure financing
excerpt: KB Kookmin Bank has secured the lead arranger role in a 12. 6 trillion won ($9. 45 billion) project to build artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure in Korea, the lender said Sunday. Led by Brookfield, one of the world’s largest alternative asset managers, the project involves acquiring major high-performance computing equipment, including graphics processing units (GPUs), and supplying the infrastructure to Naver Cloud. The deal marks the largest syndicated loan arrangement in Korea’s history. Such loans allow multiple financial institutions to jointly finance a large-scale project. It is also the country’s first GPU financing deal — a departure from conventional project financing, which has typically centered on assets like real estate or power plants. Rather than relying on immediate returns, the structure uses anticipated long-term revenue from supplying AI computing capacity to support the project's substantial upfront investment needs. Of the 12. 6 trillion won in total costs, roughly 10. 7 trillion won will be raised through loans. As lead arranger, KB Kookmin Bank is overseeing the financing structure, assembling the lending syndicate and coordinating loan terms to secure the necessary funding. Hana Bank, Shinhan Bank, Woori Bank and NH Investment & Securities are also reportedly participating in the financing. KB Kookmin Bank said it plans to expand its support for strategic high-tech industries following the deal. “This transaction is significant in that it opens up a new area of financing,” a bank official said. “We will continue to expand our support for industries driving growth ahead and contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of domestic industries by promoting productive finance. ”. Impress operates more than 110 clinics worldwide and is active in nine European markets, the European Investment Bank (EIB) announced on Tuesday. The funding will be used to increase investment in AI and strengthen Impress’s technology for diagnosing and treating patients using clear aligners — transparent orthodontic devices that straighten teeth. Impress’s platform combines in-clinic patient scanning, treatment planning and ongoing monitoring, including through the company’s mobile app. The company said it plans to target northern European markets after consolidating in Southern Europe, naming Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The deal reflects the bank’s work to support technological innovation and digitalisation in Europe, including in health technology, said María Romano, Head of the EIB Group Office in Spain. Impress’s artificial intelligence engine is powered by a database of 500,000 patients. The company said the system allows it to increase clinic efficiency tenfold and reduce in-person visits by 80%, according to Vladimir Lupenko, co-founder and chief executive of Impress.
